objectives: State the Core Web Vitals + their thresholds.
Reason about which bottleneck dominates each metric.

slides.title: Core Web Vitals, the production metrics
slides.body:
Google's Core Web Vitals (CWV) — the three metrics that matter for both UX + SEO:

1. **LCP (Largest Contentful Paint)**: time to render the largest visible element. Target: ≤ 2.5s. Driven by: server response, render-blocking resources, image load time.
2. **FID/INP (First Input Delay → Interaction to Next Paint)**: time from user interaction to visual response. Target: ≤ 200ms INP. Driven by: main-thread blocking, JS execution time, layout work after interaction.
3. **CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift)**: how much content moves around after initial render. Target: ≤ 0.1. Driven by: late-loading images without dimensions, fonts swapping, ad insertions.

Google uses these in search ranking signals + reports them via PageSpeed Insights, CrUX (Chrome User Experience Report — real-user data), Search Console.

Production tracking: instrument via the `web-vitals` library; report to your analytics. Watch p75 across real users, not lab numbers.

slides.title: LCP optimization checklist
slides.body:
**LCP target**: ≤ 2.5s on p75 real-user. Top contributors:

1. **Server response time (TTFB)**: anything above ~500ms is too much. Fix via CDN, faster origin, edge caching.
2. **Render-blocking resources**: synchronous `<script>` and `<link rel=stylesheet>` block render. Defer scripts (`async`, `defer`, `type='module'`). Inline critical CSS; defer non-critical.
3. **LCP image**: if largest element is an image, preload it with `<link rel='preload' as='image' fetchpriority='high'>`. Use modern formats (AVIF, WebP). Serve responsive sizes via `srcset`.
4. **Font-loading strategy**: `font-display: swap` shows fallback immediately + swaps when the web font loads. Avoids waiting on font download to paint LCP.
5. **No render-blocking JS for above-the-fold**: hydrate progressively if SSR.

Production-tier sites consistently hit LCP < 1s by combining all of these. The marginal improvement past 2.5s correlates with conversion-rate improvement.

slides.title: Lazy loading + code splitting
slides.body: Code splitting: ship only the JS/CSS needed for the current page, not your whole app. Modern bundlers (Vite, esbuild, webpack 5+, Next.js) do this automatically per-route. ```js // Dynamic import: a separate chunk const Settings = lazy(() => import('./Settings')); }> ``` For images: - `` — defer load until near-viewport. - For above-fold images: don't lazy-load (delays LCP); preload instead. For CSS: inline critical (above-fold) CSS, defer the rest. For third-party scripts (analytics, ads, chat widgets): defer or lazy-load. They're usually the #1 cause of slow INP because they load + execute on the main thread. Production rule: every kilobyte of JS shipped is a kilobyte of work the main thread does. Cut bytes, cut latency.

question.question: Derive a JS budget from device + network specs
question.goal: Target: LCP < 2.5s on median mobile (3G, low-end Android). What's the JS budget?

steps.prompt: Median mobile: ~1.6 Mbps effective bandwidth = 200 KB/s. Plus per-chunk processing time on a low-end Android CPU: ~1 KB/ms. JS lifecycle: download → parse → compile → execute. Total time for $X$ KB?
hints: Download time + execution time. Combined cost per KB is roughly 1/167 seconds.
steps.reveal: Roughly $X/167$ seconds per KB on median mobile (download + execute).

steps.prompt: Budget: 2.5s LCP, with say 1s reserved for non-JS work. So JS has ~1.5s. Max $X$?
steps.reveal: ~250 KB total JS budget. Many sites ship 2-5 MB; that's why mobile is slow.

question.finalResult: $$\boxed{\text{JS budget: } \sim 250\text{ KB to hit LCP < 2.5s on median mobile}}$$ Brutal but real. Code-split aggressively, defer non-critical, audit third-party scripts. The web isn't ImageMagick on a 10-year-old laptop — but median user devices are similar.

question.question: Your site's CLS is 0.4 (target: ≤ 0.1). Most likely cause:
options: Images are loaded without explicit dimensions, so the layout shifts when they finally arrive.
question.explanation: CLS is about layout shift — content moving around after initial render. The classic cause: `` without `width` + `height` attributes, so the layout reserves no space; when the image arrives, content below jumps. Fix: always include width + height on images (or `aspect-ratio` CSS). Same applies to ads + late-injected widgets.

hints: Images without dimensions don't reserve space; when they arrive, layout reflows.
slides.workedSolution: CLS = layout shift. Loading images without `width`+`height` (or CSS `aspect-ratio`) means the layout reserves 0 height for them; when they arrive, content below jumps down. Fix: always specify dimensions. Same for embedded media, ads, late-injected components. Modern frameworks (Next.js Image, Astro `<Image/>`) enforce dimensions by default.

Pinpointing a slow LCP
question.prompt: Lighthouse reports LCP = 4.5s on your homepage (way above target). Walk through your debug + remediation plan.
Explain in two or three sentences why mobile-first performance budgets are far stricter than desktop budgets in 2025.
question.rubric: Mentions that median global users are on cheap Android with intermittent 3G/4G; CPU is ~5× slower than mid-range desktop; bandwidth often <2 Mbps; the same code that runs at 60fps on a Mac runs at 5fps on a $100 phone in rural India.
